claims.source: ASIC1a belongs to the H+-gated subgroup of the degenerin/epithelial Na+ channel (DEG/ENaC) family of non-selective cation channels, widely expressed in central (CNS) and peripheral (PNS) nervous systems (Wemmie et al., 2006, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wemmie et al., 2006, 2013.

claims.claim: ASIC1a is an effective molecular target for mitigating acid-induced neural damage in multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease, and Parkinson's disease.
claims.source: To date, besides ischemic stroke, accumulating evidence from cell/animal models shows that ASIC1a is an effective molecular target for mitigating acid-induced neural damage in many other diseases including multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease, and Parkinson's disease (Wemmie et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wemmie et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Ca2+ influx through homomeric ASIC1a channels has been traditionally considered to be the main cause of acidotoxicity.
claims.source: Traditionally, Ca2+ influx through homomeric ASIC1a channels has been considered to be the main cause of acidotoxicity (Xiong et al., 2004; Yermolaieva et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Xiong et al., 2004 and Yermolaieva et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Homomeric ASIC1a channels are completely desensitized after just a few seconds of continued exposure to extracellular acid.
claims.source: First, homomeric ASIC1a channels are completely desensitized after just a few seconds of continued exposure to extracellular acid, a phenomenon termed steady-state desensitization (Krishtal, 2003; Duan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Krishtal, 2003 and Duan et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The Ca2+ permeability of ASIC1a channels is relatively small compared to many other Ca2+-permeable channels, such as NMDA receptors.
claims.source: Second, compared to many other Ca2+-permeable channels, such as NMDA receptors, the Ca2+ permeability of ASIC1a channels is relatively small (Samways et al., 2009; Wang and Xu, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Samways et al., 2009 and Wang and Xu, 2011.

claims.claim: RIP1 was identified as the crucial mediator of necroptosis, with RIP1 phosphorylation being the key step.
claims.source: Recently, the serine/threonine kinase receptor interaction protein 1 (RIP1) was identified as the crucial mediator of this process, with RIP1 phosphorylation being the key step in necroptosis (Degterev et al., 2005; Christofferson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Degterev et al., 2005 and Christofferson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Blockade of RIP1 phosphorylation by necrostatin-1 (Nec-1) inhibited necroptosis.
claims.source: Blockade of RIP1 phosphorylation by the specific inhibitor, necrostatin-1 (Nec-1), inhibited necroptosis (Degterev et al., 2005; Christofferson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Degterev et al., 2005 and Christofferson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Neurons treated with pH 6.0 solution displayed a typical necrotic phenotype including plasma membrane rupture, organelle swelling, and cell lysis.
claims.source: those treated with a pH 6.0 solution (1 hr treatment and 24 hr recovery in normal culture medium, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, middle panel) displayed a typical necrotic phenotype (Kroemer et al., 2009), including plasma membrane rupture, organelle swelling, and cell lysis (Figure 1A1, middle and right panels; Figure 1A2, lower panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1A1 and 1A2.

claims.claim: Of 57 cells counted in the pH 6.0-treated samples, 47 showed necrotic morphology.
claims.source: Of 57 cells counted in the pH 6.0-treated samples, 47 showed morphology similar to that shown in the middle and right panels.
claims.evidence: This is quantitative data from electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 1A1.

claims.claim: For pH 7.4-treated samples, only 3 out of 41 cells examined showed morphology resembling necrotic cells.
claims.source: For pH 7.4-treated samples, the majority of cells had a similar morphology to that shown in the left panel; only 3 out of the 41 cells examined showed morphology that resembled that in the middle panel.
claims.evidence: This is quantitative data from electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 1A1.

claims.claim: PcTX1 (10 nM) rescued cells from acid-induced neuronal death.
claims.source: PcTX1 (10 nM) and Nec-1 (20 μM), but not BHA (100 μM), BEL (30 μM), DPI (15 μM), RTO (25 μM), CHX (100 μM), or z-VAD-fmk (10 μM), rescued cells from acid-induced neuronal death (indicated by the dashed line) (n=4–12, ***p<0.001; NS, no statistical significance, vs vehicle (Veh) at pH 6.0).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Nec-1 (20 μM) rescued cells from acid-induced neuronal death.
claims.source: PcTX1 (10 nM) and Nec-1 (20 μM), but not BHA (100 μM), BEL (30 μM), DPI (15 μM), RTO (25 μM), CHX (100 μM), or z-VAD-fmk (10 μM), rescued cells from acid-induced neuronal death (indicated by the dashed line) (n=4–12, ***p<0.001; NS, no statistical significance, vs vehicle (Veh) at pH 6.0).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: BHA (100 μM) did not rescue cells from acid-induced neuronal death.
claims.source: PcTX1 (10 nM) and Nec-1 (20 μM), but not BHA (100 μM), BEL (30 μM), DPI (15 μM), RTO (25 μM), CHX (100 μM), or z-VAD-fmk (10 μM), rescued cells from acid-induced neuronal death (indicated by the dashed line) (n=4–12, ***p<0.001; NS, no statistical significance, vs vehicle (Veh) at pH 6.0).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: z-VAD-fmk (10 μM) did not rescue cells from acid-induced neuronal death.
claims.source: PcTX1 (10 nM) and Nec-1 (20 μM), but not BHA (100 μM), BEL (30 μM), DPI (15 μM), RTO (25 μM), CHX (100 μM), or z-VAD-fmk (10 μM), rescued cells from acid-induced neuronal death (indicated by the dashed line) (n=4–12, ***p<0.001; NS, no statistical significance, vs vehicle (Veh) at pH 6.0).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The IC50 of Nec-1 for rescuing acid-induced neuronal death is 12.6 μM.
claims.source: To our surprise, however, inhibiting RIP1 phosphorylation (Figure 2A,B) by Nec-1 (Degterev et al., 2005) also resulted in a similar protective effect (IC50, 12.6 μM, Figure 1B; CTB assay).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1B inset.

claims.claim: Nec-1 (20 μM) rescued neurons from acid-induced death as measured by propidium iodide staining.
claims.source: Rescue from acid-induced neuronal death by 20 μM Nec-1 (propidium iodide [PI] staining assay).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 1C1 and 1C2.

claims.claim: RIP1 shRNA significantly reduced RIP1 protein expression compared to β-Gal control.
claims.source: Knockdown efficiency of RIP1 shRNA as determined by Western blotting (***p<0.001, vs β-Gal).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: RIP1 shRNA rescued neurons from acid-induced death.
claims.source: Rescue of acid-induced neuronal death by RIP1 shRNA (CTB assay, n=3, ***p<0.001; NS, no statistical significance, vs β-Gal at pH 7.4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The activity of caspase 8 was moderately increased 4 and 8 hr after pH 6.0 treatment.
claims.source: Although the activity of caspase 8 was moderately increased 4 and 8 hr after the pH 6.0 treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), that of executive apoptosis effectors, caspase 3/7, did not increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by caspase activity assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Caspase 3/7 activities did not increase after pH 6.0 treatment.
claims.source: Although the activity of caspase 8 was moderately increased 4 and 8 hr after the pH 6.0 treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), that of executive apoptosis effectors, caspase 3/7, did not increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by caspase activity assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: Cleavage of caspase 3 was undetectable by Western blotting after pH 6.0 treatment.
claims.source: Rather, caspase 3/7 activities decreased slightly at 4 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and the cleavage of caspase 3 (activated caspase 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) was undetectable by Western blotting.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Acid triggers necrotic neuronal death but not apoptosis under the experimental conditions used.
claims.source: These data, together with the result that pan caspase inhibitor z-VAD-fmk failed to block pH 6.0-induced neuronal death (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), suggest that acid triggers necrotic neuronal death but not apoptosis under the current experimental conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental results including caspase assays and z-VAD-fmk treatment.

claims.claim: Nec-1 did not affect acid (pH 6.0)-evoked currents in neurons with up to 30 min pretreatment.
claims.source: Unlike PcTX1, up to 30 min pretreatment with Nec-1 did not affect the acid (pH 6.0)-evoked currents (I6.0) in the neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: pH 6.0 treatment resulted in no obvious change in ROS levels in neurons.
claims.source: However, the pH 6.0 treatment resulted in no obvious change in ROS levels in the neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and neither scavenging ROS by anti-oxidant butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) nor blockade of ROS production by rotenone (RTO) or diphenylene iodonium (DPI) rescued neurons from acid-induced death (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: 30 min treatment with pH 6.0 solution significantly increased RIP1 phosphorylation as measured by 32P incorporation.
claims.source: Both methods showed significant increases in RIP1 phosphorylation upon 30 min treatment with the pH 6.0 solution, which were suppressed by Nec-1 (Figure 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 32P incorporation data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Acid-induced RIP1 phosphorylation was suppressed by Nec-1.
claims.source: Both methods showed significant increases in RIP1 phosphorylation upon 30 min treatment with the pH 6.0 solution, which were suppressed by Nec-1 (Figure 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: Acid-induced RIP1 phosphorylation was inhibited by PcTX1.
claims.source: Consistent with ASIC1a being critical for necrotic cell death and upstream of RIP1 activation, acid-induced RIP1 phosphorylation was inhibited by PcTX1 (Figure 2B) and was undetectable in neurons from Asic1a−/− mice (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Acid-induced RIP1 phosphorylation was undetectable in neurons from Asic1a−/− mice.
claims.source: Consistent with ASIC1a being critical for necrotic cell death and upstream of RIP1 activation, acid-induced RIP1 phosphorylation was inhibited by PcTX1 (Figure 2B) and was undetectable in neurons from Asic1a−/− mice (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Reducing the pH of the reaction solution to 6.0 did not alter RIP1 phosphorylation in an in vitro cell-free phosphorylation assay.
claims.source: To rule out the possibility that acid-induced RIP1 phosphorylation resulted from intracellular acidification, we performed an in vitro cell-free phosphorylation assay and found that reducing the pH of the reaction solution to 6.0 did not alter RIP1 phosphorylation (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Extracellular acid-induced intracellular acidification was similar between neurons from Asic1a+/+ and Asic1a−/− mice.
claims.source: Moreover, despite similar extracellular acid-induced intracellular acidification between neurons from Asic1a+/+ (wild type, WT) and Asic1a−/− mice (Figure 2D1,D2), only WT, but not Asic1a−/−, neurons showed enhanced RIP1 phosphorylation in response to the extracellular pH reduction (Figure 2C), suggesting that the presence of ASIC1a proteins rather than intracellular acidification was necessary for such a response.
claims.evidence: This is supported by BCECF imaging data shown in Figure 2D1 and 2D2.

claims.claim: The total protein level of RIP1 was increased in the first 30 min of acidosis treatment and then declined to ∼80% of the basal level at 60 min.
claims.source: Interestingly, the total protein level of RIP1 was also increased in the first 30 min of acidosis treatment and then declined to ∼80% of the basal level at 60 min (Figure 2F1,F2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F1 and 2F2.

claims.claim: RIP1 was recruited to ASIC1a in mouse cortical neurons after 30 min treatment with pH 6.0 solution.
claims.source: Furthermore and possibly related to the acid-induced increase in RIP1 phosphorylation, we found that RIP1 was recruited to ASIC1a in mouse cortical neurons after 30 min treatment with the pH 6.0 solution (Figure 2G1,G2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A1,A2) and that this effect was suppressed by PcTX1 (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2G1 and 2G2.

claims.claim: Acid-induced ASIC1a-RIP1 association was suppressed by PcTX1.
claims.source: Furthermore and possibly related to the acid-induced increase in RIP1 phosphorylation, we found that RIP1 was recruited to ASIC1a in mouse cortical neurons after 30 min treatment with the pH 6.0 solution (Figure 2G1,G2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A1,A2) and that this effect was suppressed by PcTX1 (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: The protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) failed to protect neurons from acid-induced death.
claims.source: To evaluate the possibility that acid-induced necroptosis arose from autocrine production of cytokines, we first tested whether de novo protein synthesis was required for cell death and found that the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) failed to protect neurons from acid-induced death (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: TNF-α neutralizing antibody failed to rescue neurons from acid-induced death.
claims.source: Second, we used the TNF-α neutralizing antibody but found that it failed to rescue neurons from acid-induced death, while it was effective in protecting neurons from TNF-α-induced death (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: TNF-α neutralizing antibody was effective in protecting neurons from TNF-α-induced death.
claims.source: Second, we used the TNF-α neutralizing antibody but found that it failed to rescue neurons from acid-induced death, while it was effective in protecting neurons from TNF-α-induced death (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Two-minute superfusion with pH 7.2 or pH 6.8 solution drastically reduced I6.0 by approximately 60% or 90%, respectively.
claims.source: Just 2 min superfusion with the pH 7.2 or pH 6.8 solution drastically reduced I6.0 by approximately 60% or 90%, respectively (Figure 3A1,A2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3A1 and 3A2.

claims.claim: Pretreatment of neurons with pH 6.8 solution failed to inhibit acid-induced neuronal death.
claims.source: In contrast, pretreatment of neurons with pH 6.8 solution failed to inhibit acid-induced neuronal death (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that ASIC1a channels were able to mediate acidotoxicity even under steady-state desensitized conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The number of PI-positive neurons continued to increase with increasing durations of pH 6.0 treatment in cultures prepared from Asic1a+/+ mice.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, the number of PI-positive neurons continued to increase with increasing durations of the pH 6.0 treatment in cultures prepared from Asic1a+/+ mice, indicating that despite the nearly complete channel desensitization throughout the major part (except for the first few seconds) of the 1 hr treatment, acid continued to exert an effect on neuronal death.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Acid treatment failed to induce significant neuronal death in cultures prepared from Asic1a−/− mice for all treatment durations.
claims.source: On the other hand, consistent with previous findings (Xiong et al., 2004; Duan et al., 2011), acid treatment failed to induce significant neuronal death in cultures prepared from Asic1a−/− mice for all treatment durations (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating that despite the lack of proton-induced current, the neuronal death induced by persistent acidosis was still dependent on the presence of ASIC1a.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Application of pH 6.0 solution to cultured mouse cortical neurons elicited a rise in intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies, application of the pH 6.0 solution to the cultured mouse cortical neurons elicited a rise in intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i), which was significantly reduced following inhibition of ionotropic glutamate receptors and voltage-gated Na+ and Ca2+ channels, while the remaining response was largely blocked by PcTX1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A1,A2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Fura-2 Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A1 and 2A2.

claims.claim: The Ca2+ response to pH 6.0 was not detected in neurons from Asic1a−/− mice.
claims.source: The Ca2+ response was not detected in neurons from Asic1a−/− mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B1), but restored with the transient expression of ASIC1a cDNA in these neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B2,B4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Fura-2 Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B1.

claims.claim: A Ca2+-free pH 6.0 solution induced neuronal death to a similar level as the normal Ca2+-containing pH 6.0 solution.
claims.source: Indeed, a Ca2+-free pH 6.0 solution (with no Ca2+ added and the addition of 10 mM EGTA), which would not support Ca2+ influx, induced neuronal death to a similar level as the normal Ca2+-containing pH 6.0 solution (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Acid-induced neuronal death in the Ca2+-free condition was inhibited by PcTX1 and Nec-1s.
claims.source: Importantly, acid-induced neuronal death in the Ca2+-free condition was also inhibited by PcTX1 and Nec-1s (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), indicating the involvement of the ASIC1a-RIP pathway despite the lack of Ca2+ influx.
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Depletion of extracellular Ca2+ did not reduce I6.0 in cultured mouse cortical neurons.
claims.source: Notably, unlike I6.0 in ASIC1a-transfected CHO cells (Duan et al., 2011), depletion of extracellular Ca2+ did not reduce I6.0 in cultured mouse cortical neurons (Figure 3E), suggestive of a different modulatory mechanism exerted on native ASIC1a by extracellular Ca2+ under the present experimental conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Replacement of Na+, K+, and Ca2+ with NMDG resulted in no detectable I6.0 but acid still resulted in marked neuronal death.
claims.source: To further examine the contribution of ion influx to acid-induced neuronal death, we replaced Na+, K+, and Ca2+ in the treatment solution with an impermanent cation, N-methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG), keeping osmolarity unchanged. Under these conditions, no I6.0 was detected because of the lack of permeant ions (Figure 3E), but acid still resulted in marked neuronal death (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology and CTB assay data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: Co-administration of amiloride (AMI) with acid significantly inhibited I6.0 but did not show neuroprotection.
claims.source: We also tested the non-specific ASIC blocker, amiloride (AMI), which acts by blocking the channel pore. Although co-administration of AMI with acid significantly inhibited I6.0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B1,B2), it did not show neuroprotection (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology and CTB assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with AMI for 1 hr before acid stimulation largely prevented acidotoxicity.
claims.source: Interestingly, if neurons were pretreated with AMI for 1 hr before acid stimulation, the acidotoxicity was largely prevented (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C), suggesting that pretreatment with AMI may modulate the ASIC1a channel with a different mechanism beyond the channel blockade.
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claims.claim: HIF-ASIC1a (32HIF34 mutated to 32AAA34) was ion non-conducting due to pore dysfunction.
claims.source: While both were expressed normally on the plasma membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), HIF-ASIC1a (32HIF34 mutated to 32AAA34) was ion non-conducting due to pore dysfunction (Pfister et al., 2006) (Figure 3F,G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F and 3G, and citation to Pfister et al., 2006.

claims.claim: RC-ASIC1a was electrophysiologically functional as the WT channel.
claims.source: RC-ASIC1a was electrophysiologically functional as the WT channel (Figure 3F), but its C-terminus (R462-C526) was replaced by a shortened scrambled amino acid sequence, KLRILQSTVPRARDDPDLDN (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Both WT-ASIC1a and the ion non-conducting HIF mutant, but not the conducting RC mutant, restored acid-induced death in Asic1a−/− neurons.
claims.source: By expressing WT-ASIC1a, HIF-ASIC1a, or RC-ASIC1a in cortical neurons from Asic1a−/− mice, we found that both WT-ASIC1a and the ion non-conducting HIF mutant, but not the conducting RC mutant, restored the acid-induced death in Asic1a−/− neurons (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 6), although both WT- and RC-ASIC1a, but not the HIF mutant, restored the Ca2+ response to fast focal perfusion with the pH 6.0 solution (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B2–B4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: CHO cells expressing homomeric ASIC1a failed to yield a [Ca2+]i rise in response to acid.
claims.source: Furthermore, although CHO cells expressing homomeric ASIC1a failed to yield a [Ca2+]i rise in response to acid (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A1,A2), the stable expression of WT-ASIC1a and HIF-ASIC1a, but not RC-ASIC1a, in CHO cells also led to significant increases in acid-induced cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Fluo-4 Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A1 and 7A2.

claims.claim: Stable expression of WT-ASIC1a and HIF-ASIC1a, but not RC-ASIC1a, in CHO cells led to significant increases in acid-induced cell death.
claims.source: Furthermore, although CHO cells expressing homomeric ASIC1a failed to yield a [Ca2+]i rise in response to acid (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A1,A2), the stable expression of WT-ASIC1a and HIF-ASIC1a, but not RC-ASIC1a, in CHO cells also led to significant increases in acid-induced cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7B.

claims.claim: pH 6.0 solution treatment caused ASIC1a–RIP1 association in CHO cells that expressed ASIC1a.
claims.source: Supporting a similar ASIC1a/RIP1-mediated death mechanism in CHO cells as in neurons, pH 6.0 solution treatment also caused ASIC1a–RIP1 association in CHO cells that expressed ASIC1a (Figure 3—figure supplement 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7C.

claims.claim: ASIC1b mediated acid-induced death when expressed in CHO cells.
claims.source: Further supporting the importance of the ASIC1a C-terminus in acid-induced necroptosis, we found that ASIC1b, a splice variant differing from ASIC1a only at the N-terminus, also mediated acid-induced death when expressed in CHO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 7D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7D.

claims.claim: Expression of ASIC2a and ASIC3 did not restore the acid-induced death of CHO cells.
claims.source: In contrast, the expression of ASIC2a and ASIC3, which have very different C-terminal sequences from ASIC1a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), did not restore the acid-induced death of CHO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 7D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7D.

claims.claim: Homomeric ASIC1b is Ca2+ impermeable.
claims.source: Because homomeric ASIC1b is Ca2+ impermeable (Bassler et al., 2001), this finding also supports the argument that Ca2+ entry through ASIC1a is not critical for acid-induced cell death under the present experimental conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Bassler et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Incubation of mouse cortical neurons with CP-1 (10 µM, 24 hr) at physiological pH 7.4 induced cell death.
claims.source: Interestingly, incubation of mouse cortical neurons with CP-1 (10 µM, 24 hr), but not CP-2, CP-3, or CP-4, at the physiological pH 7.4, induced cell death (Figure 4B) and enhanced RIP1 phosphorylation (Figure 4C), which were both rescued, at least partially, by Nec-1 (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: CP-1 enhanced RIP1 phosphorylation at pH 7.4.
claims.source: Interestingly, incubation of mouse cortical neurons with CP-1 (10 µM, 24 hr), but not CP-2, CP-3, or CP-4, at the physiological pH 7.4, induced cell death (Figure 4B) and enhanced RIP1 phosphorylation (Figure 4C), which were both rescued, at least partially, by Nec-1 (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Nec-1 (20 µM) at least partially rescued CP-1-induced cell death and RIP1 phosphorylation.
claims.source: Interestingly, incubation of mouse cortical neurons with CP-1 (10 µM, 24 hr), but not CP-2, CP-3, or CP-4, at the physiological pH 7.4, induced cell death (Figure 4B) and enhanced RIP1 phosphorylation (Figure 4C), which were both rescued, at least partially, by Nec-1 (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay and phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claims.claim: CP-1 peptide caused the death of CHO cells, which do not endogenously express ASIC1a.
claims.source: Moreover, the CP-1 peptide caused the death of CHO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), which do not endogenously express ASIC1a, suggesting that its toxicity does not require full-length ASIC1a.
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: A physical association between RIP1 and ASIC1a was detected only in the ischemic hemisphere but not the control hemisphere of the same brain.
claims.source: Supporting the role of ASIC1a in mediating RIP1 activation in ischemic brain damage, we detected a physical association between RIP1 and ASIC1a only in the ischemic hemisphere but not the control hemisphere of the same brain (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from MCAO mouse brains shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: 30 min MCAO was sufficient to induce ASIC1a-RIP1 association.
claims.source: Importantly, 30 min MCAO, which was too short to cause obvious brain damage as shown by TTL staining (Figure 5C), was sufficient to induce the ASIC1a-RIP1 association.
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B and TTC staining shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: ASIC1a-RIP1 association persisted for up to at least 2 hr after MCAO.
claims.source: Such association persisted for up to at least 2 hr (Figure 5D), the longest duration of MCAO tested (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The total protein level of RIP1 tended to decrease in the ischemic side of the brain.
claims.source: Interestingly, the total protein level of RIP1 tended to decrease in the ischemic side of the brain (Figure 5D), similar to that observed in cultured cortical neurons subjected to acid treatment (Figure 2F1,F2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Increased RIP1 phosphorylation was observed in ischemic brain from WT mice.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports (Degterev et al., 2005, 2008), we observed increased RIP1 phosphorylation in ischemic brain from WT mice, which was successfully removed by treating the RIP1 immunoprecipitant for 1 hr with a bovine intestinal alkaline phosphatase (Figure 5E, upper).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 5E upper panel.

claims.claim: The level of RIP1 phosphorylation in the ischemic hemisphere of Asic1a−/− mice remained unchanged compared to the control hemisphere.
claims.source: By contrast, the level of RIP1 phosphorylation in the ischemic hemisphere of the Asic1a−/− mice remained unchanged as compared to the control hemisphere (Figure 5E, lower), demonstrating the critical role of ASIC1a in ischemia-induced RIP1 activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 5E lower panel.

claims.claim: ASIC1a-dependent necroptosis does not require de novo synthesized ligands.
claims.source: Compared to conventional DR-dependent necroptosis, ASIC1a-dependent necroptosis did not require de novo synthesized ligands and extracellular protons may serve as the fast 'extrinsic death signal'.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the CHX experiment showing no requirement for protein synthesis.

claims.claim: ASIC1a-dependent necroptosis does not require intrinsic ROS generation.

claims.evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data and lack of protection by ROS scavengers.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Xiong et al., 2004.

claims.claim: The ion-conducting function of ASIC1a channels appears to not be essential for acid-induced necroptotic cell death.
claims.source: Here we show the indispensible role of ASIC1a channels in mediating neuronal necroptosis in response to extracellular acidification, but the ion-conducting function of the ASIC1a channels appears to not be essential for this process.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings including HIF mutant experiments.

claims.claim: RIP1 activation but not ionic conduction per se is necessary for acid-induced necroptotic cell death.
claims.source: Although it cannot be ruled out that ionic fluxes through the channel pore may play a modulatory role, our data suggest that RIP1 activation but not ionic conduction per se is necessary for acid-induced necroptotic cell death (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: The acid-induced conformational change in ASIC1a channels exposes its proximal C-terminal region to trigger RIP1 phosphorylation.
claims.source: Since ion channel activation reflects conformational changes induced by ligands and other gating factors, it is plausible that the acid-induced conformational change in ASIC1a channels exposes its proximal C-terminal region, represented by the CP-1 peptide (Figure 4), to trigger RIP1 phosphorylation (Figure 5F) and the consequent neuronal necroptosis in response to tissue acidosis.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Steady-state desensitization of the ASIC1a channel by moderate pH decreases did not prevent acid-induced neuronal death.
claims.source: Ironically, steady-state desensitization of the ASIC1a channel by moderate pH decreases, although it suppressed subsequent activation of ASIC1a current, did not prevent acid-induced neuronal death (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: PcTX1 inhibits both the C-terminal RIP1 activation domain exposure and channel gating.
claims.source: Presumably, extracellular protons cause at least two steps in conformational changes in ASIC1a: one that exposes the C-terminal RIP1 activation domain and the other that mediates channel gating. Only the latter is blocked by the steady-state desensitization induced by the moderated pH decrease, whereas both are inhibited by PcTX1, especially because of the presence of PcTX1 throughout the entire period of pH 6.0 treatment.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: AMI was protective against neuronal death when applied before, but not during acidosis.
claims.source: Consistent with the two-step conformational changes, AMI was protective against neuronal death when applied before, but not during acidosis, which differed from its action in blocking channel conductance (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CTB assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

results.result: Acid treatment (pH 6.0) induces necrotic neuronal death characterized by plasma membrane rupture, organelle swelling, and cell lysis, without activating apoptotic pathways. Electron microscopy showed 47 of 57 pH 6.0-treated neurons displayed necrotic morphology versus 3 of 41 control neurons. Caspase 3/7 activities did not increase and caspase 3 cleavage was undetectable, while the pan-caspase inhibitor z-VAD-fmk failed to prevent death.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary approaches (electron microscopy morphology C19-C21, caspase activity assays C30-C32, and pharmacological inhibition C25) consistently demonstrate necrotic rather than apoptotic death. The quantitative data are robust with adequate sample sizes, and the conclusion (C33) logically follows from the experimental evidence.

results.result: Both PcTX1 (ASIC1a inhibitor) and Nec-1 (RIP1 inhibitor) rescue neurons from acid-induced death. Nec-1 showed dose-dependent protection with IC50 of 12.6 μM, and RIP1 knockdown by shRNA also prevented acid-induced neuronal death.
results.evaluation: The protective effects are demonstrated through multiple independent methods (pharmacological inhibition C22-C23, C26-C27 and genetic knockdown C28-C29) using different assays (CTB and PI staining). The dose-response relationship for Nec-1 strengthens the claim. Statistical significance is reported (p<0.001) with adequate replicates (n=4-12).

results.result: Acid treatment induces RIP1 phosphorylation in an ASIC1a-dependent manner that requires the presence of ASIC1a protein but not intracellular acidification. RIP1 phosphorylation was detected by two independent methods (32P incorporation and phospho-S/T antibody), was blocked by PcTX1 and Nec-1, and was absent in Asic1a−/− neurons despite similar intracellular acidification.
results.evaluation: The use of two independent phosphorylation detection methods (C36) strengthens the findings. The genetic (C39) and pharmacological (C37-C38) controls are appropriate. The cell-free assay (C40) and intracellular pH measurements (C41) effectively rule out intracellular acidification as the mechanism, supporting the conclusion that ASIC1a protein presence is required.

results.result: Acid stimulation recruits RIP1 to ASIC1a within 30 minutes, and this association is suppressed by PcTX1. This physical interaction between ASIC1a and RIP1 is proposed to cause RIP1 phosphorylation and subsequent neuronal death.
results.evaluation: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments (C43-C44) demonstrate the physical association between ASIC1a and RIP1 following acid treatment. The temporal relationship (30 min) and PcTX1 sensitivity are well-documented. However, the causal link to RIP1 phosphorylation and death (C5) is inferential rather than directly demonstrated through mechanistic dissection.

results.result: ASIC1a channels mediate acidotoxicity even under steady-state desensitized conditions. Pretreatment with pH 6.8 reduced acid-evoked currents by ~90% but failed to prevent acid-induced neuronal death. Neuronal death increased with duration of pH 6.0 exposure in wild-type but not Asic1a−/− neurons.
results.evaluation: The electrophysiological data (C48) clearly demonstrate channel desensitization, while cell death assays (C49-C51) show continued ASIC1a-dependent toxicity. The time-course experiment (C50) is particularly compelling, showing progressive death despite channel desensitization. This strongly challenges the traditional Ca2+ influx hypothesis and is a key finding of the paper.

results.result: Acid-induced neuronal death occurs independently of Ca2+ influx and ionic conduction through ASIC1a. Ca2+-free conditions induced similar death levels as Ca2+-containing solutions, and replacement of all permeant ions with NMDG eliminated currents but not death. Amiloride co-treatment blocked currents without providing protection, though pretreatment was protective.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary ionic manipulation experiments (C54, C57) consistently show death occurs without ion flux. The PcTX1/Nec-1s protection in Ca2+-free conditions (C55) confirms ASIC1a-RIP1 pathway involvement. The amiloride experiments (C58-C59) are particularly informative, distinguishing channel blockade from other modulatory effects. The data strongly support ion-independent mechanisms.

results.result: The ion-conducting function of ASIC1a is not essential for acid-induced necroptotic death. Expression of the non-conducting HIF-ASIC1a mutant restored acid-induced death in Asic1a−/− neurons, while the conducting RC-ASIC1a mutant (with scrambled C-terminus) did not. Similar results were obtained in CHO cells, which showed no Ca2+ response to acid.
results.evaluation: The mutant rescue experiments (C62) provide strong evidence for ion-independent mechanisms. The HIF mutant is well-characterized as non-conducting (C60, with citation), and the RC mutant serves as an appropriate control showing that conductance alone is insufficient (C61). The CHO cell experiments (C63-C64) extend findings to a non-neuronal system. This is a central finding supporting the paper's main conclusion (C89).

results.result: The C-terminus of ASIC1a is critical for acid-induced death. ASIC1b (differing only at N-terminus) mediated death in CHO cells, while ASIC2a and ASIC3 (with different C-termini) did not. Since ASIC1b is Ca2+-impermeable, this further supports Ca2+-independent mechanisms.
results.evaluation: The ASIC isoform comparison (C66-C67) provides strong structure-function evidence for C-terminal involvement. The ASIC1b result (C66, C68) is particularly compelling as it simultaneously demonstrates C-terminal importance and Ca2+-independence. The negative results with ASIC2a/3 serve as appropriate controls.

results.result: A synthetic peptide (CP-1) representing the proximal C-terminus of ASIC1a (residues 468-483) mimics acid-induced necroptosis. CP-1 induced neuronal death and RIP1 phosphorylation at physiological pH 7.4, effects partially rescued by Nec-1. CP-1 also caused death in CHO cells lacking endogenous ASIC1a.
results.evaluation: The CP-1 peptide experiments (C69-C71) provide functional evidence for the C-terminal region's role. The specificity is demonstrated by negative results with other peptides (CP-2, CP-3, CP-4). The CHO cell result (C72) shows the effect doesn't require full-length ASIC1a. However, the mechanism by which a TAT-tagged peptide mimics the conformational change of the full channel remains unclear and somewhat speculative.

results.result: In a mouse MCAO model of ischemic stroke, ASIC1a-RIP1 association and RIP1 phosphorylation occur in affected brain areas. This association was detected as early as 30 minutes post-MCAO and persisted for at least 2 hours. RIP1 phosphorylation was increased in wild-type but not Asic1a−/− ischemic brains, and Asic1a deletion prevented brain damage.
results.evaluation: The in vivo experiments (C73-C78) effectively translate the in vitro findings to a disease-relevant model. The time course (C74-C75) is well-characterized, and the genetic controls (C78) are appropriate. The comparison between ischemic and control hemispheres within the same brain (C73) is a strong experimental design. The data support the physiological relevance of the ASIC1a-RIP1 pathway in ischemic injury.

results.result: ASIC1a-dependent necroptosis differs mechanistically from conventional death receptor-dependent necroptosis. It does not require ROS generation, Ca2+ influx, cPLA2 activity, de novo protein synthesis, or TNF-α signaling. Nec-1 did not affect acid-evoked currents, indicating RIP1 acts downstream of ASIC1a activation.
results.evaluation: The systematic exclusion of alternative mechanisms (C24-C25, C35, C45-C47) through pharmacological and genetic approaches is thorough. The negative results with ROS scavengers (C24, C35), protein synthesis inhibitor (C45), and TNF-α antibody (C46) are well-controlled. The demonstration that Nec-1 doesn't affect currents (C34) supports the proposed pathway order. This characterization distinguishes the novel pathway from known mechanisms.

results.result: Application of pH 6.0 solution to cultured cortical neurons elicits a rise in intracellular Ca2+ that is ASIC1a-dependent. The Ca2+ response was blocked by inhibitors of glutamate receptors and voltage-gated channels, with the remaining response blocked by PcTX1. The response was absent in Asic1a−/− neurons but restored by ASIC1a expression.
results.evaluation: The Ca2+ imaging experiments (C52-C53) are well-controlled with appropriate pharmacological dissection and genetic validation. However, the authors later show this Ca2+ response requires fast perfusion and is not critical for cell death, which somewhat diminishes the importance of this finding. It serves mainly to confirm ASIC1a activation rather than to support the death mechanism.

results.result: The total protein level of RIP1 increased in the first 30 minutes of acidosis treatment and then declined to approximately 80% of basal level at 60 minutes.
results.evaluation: The Western blot data (C42) clearly show the biphasic change in RIP1 protein levels. However, the functional significance of this observation is unclear, and the mechanism is not explored. While interesting, this finding is not central to the main conclusions and may represent a secondary effect.

results.result: The proposed mechanism involves acid-induced conformational changes in ASIC1a that expose the proximal C-terminal region, triggering RIP1 phosphorylation. PcTX1 is proposed to inhibit both C-terminal domain exposure and channel gating, while steady-state desensitization only blocks gating.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic model (C91, C93) is largely speculative and based on indirect evidence. While the data support that conformational changes occur and that the C-terminus is important, direct evidence for C-terminal exposure or the proposed two-step conformational change is lacking. Structural or biophysical studies would be needed to validate this model. The claims are reasonable interpretations but remain hypothetical.

results.result: Background claims establishing that acidotoxicity is common in neurological disorders, ASIC1a is the key proton receptor, and traditional views held that Ca2+ influx through ASIC1a causes acidotoxicity. However, ASIC1a channels rapidly desensitize and have relatively low Ca2+ permeability. RIP1 is the crucial mediator of necroptosis, with phosphorylation being the key step.
results.evaluation: These are primarily literature-based background claims (C1-C2, C8-C18) supported by appropriate citations. They establish the context and rationale for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the statements accurately represent established knowledge in the field. These claims set up the paradox that motivates the current work.

results.result: Discussion of prior work showing that Asic1a deletion and Nec-1 treatment protect against ischemic injury, and that both ASIC1a and RIP1 are therapeutic targets in traumatic brain injury. The authors distinguish their findings from prior work on mitochondrial ASIC1a (mtASIC1a), which is involved in ROS-induced death.
results.evaluation: These claims (C81-C83, C85-C88) accurately cite and interpret prior literature. The distinction from mtASIC1a work (C85-C88) is important for clarifying the scope of the current findings. The citations appear appropriate and the interpretations are reasonable. This contextualizes the current work within the broader field.

results.result: Discussion of precedents for ion channel functions independent of ion conduction, including EAG K+ channels modulating cell proliferation, Na+ channel β subunits contributing to cell adhesion, GluN2B-NMDA receptors binding signaling proteins, and TRPM7 containing a kinase domain.
results.evaluation: These literature-based claims (C95-C99) provide important context showing that non-conducting functions of ion channels are not unprecedented. The citations appear appropriate and support the authors' argument that their findings fit within a broader paradigm. This strengthens the plausibility of their conclusions.

results.result: Discussion of evolutionary implications of the CP-1 sequence being non-conserved among ASIC isoforms, and speculation about potential conduction-independent roles of ASIC1a in synaptic function. The authors note that while Asic1a−/− mice show synaptic and learning deficits, the contribution of ASIC1a to synaptic currents is minimal.
results.evaluation: The evolutionary speculation (C100) is reasonable but not directly tested. The discussion of synaptic function (C101-C104) is largely speculative (C104 explicitly so) and based on apparent discrepancies in the literature. While these are interesting hypotheses for future work, they are not supported by data in the current manuscript. The speculation is reasonable but remains unvalidated.

results.result: The authors conclude that the inability to activate RIP1 explains the resistance of Asic1a−/− mice to ischemic brain damage, and that RIP1 activation rather than ionic conduction is necessary for acid-induced necroptotic cell death.
results.evaluation: These summary conclusions (C84, C90) are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence presented in the paper. The genetic data showing lack of RIP1 phosphorylation in Asic1a−/− mice (C39, C78) combined with the mutant rescue experiments (C62) and ionic manipulation studies (C54-C57) provide strong support. These represent the main conclusions of the work.
